You are a debugging assistant. You have access to the source code of the system under test (SUT), the failing test case (signature + snippet), the current issue report describing the failure, and several recent issue reports that have been pre-filtered by an external semantic retrieval model (SBERT) to be the most relevant to this failure among recent reports.

Your task is to provide a step-by-step explanation of how the bug occurred using all available evidence:
– the failing test (signature + snippet),
– the current bug report,
– likely-relevant recent bug reports,
– and code snippets of methods from the SUT.
Treat "likely-relevant recent bug reports" as secondary evidence: they may or may not be relevant. Use them only if they help; otherwise, you may ignore them.

Some identifiers in the current bug report may be anonymized with placeholders (e.g., C#.M#). If the same token (e.g., C1) appears multiple times, it consistently refers to the same class (C) or method (M) throughout the report. These tokens are not complete qualified names. Always confirm actual identifiers by inspecting the source code using get_code_snippet.

You will be given 9 opportunities to interact with functions to gather information for the debugging. An example diagnosis would look like follows.

Title: Diagnosis
Details: The corresponding issue report describes that tooltip text in the UI is displayed with HTML entities such as " instead of the intended characters. This strongly suggests a missing escaping or decoding step in tooltip generation. Inspecting the implementation of StandardToolTipTagFragmentGenerator.generateToolTipFragment reveals that it directly returns the toolTipText without applying any escaping. Recent issue reports mention similar encoding or escaping problems in related UI components, reinforcing the suspicion that this method lacks proper handling. The behavior observed in the code matches the issue report's symptoms, indicating that missing escaping in this method is the likely root cause.

After providing this diagnosis, you will be prompted to suggest which methods would be the best locations to be fixed. The answers should be in the form of `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` without commentary (one per line), as your answer will be automatically processed before finally being presented to the user.

Diagnosis:
The test case `testUnsafeDeSerialization` checks that deserialization of a MultiValueMap throws an `UnsupportedOperationException` when the MultiValueMap is created with a "collection type" class argument considered unsafe, in this case `String.class`. The first part of the test succeeds by serializing and deserializing a MultiValueMap constructed with `ArrayList.class` as the collection class. The second attempt is expected to fail for deserialization due to the unsafe class choice.

Looking at the code:
- The `MultiValueMap.multiValueMap(Map, Class)` factory method creates a new MultiValueMap instance with a supplied map and a collection class type, wrapping it inside a `ReflectionFactory`.
- The `ReflectionFactory.create()` method instantiates new collections by calling `clazz.newInstance()`, which means the MultiValueMap relies on creating new instances of the collection class by reflection.
- The MultiValueMap has `readObject(ObjectInputStream)` to customize deserialization, but it just calls `defaultReadObject()` and reads the map.
- The test's expectation on deserialization failure likely relates to some added safety check or restriction in the MultiValueMap or ReflectionFactory during deserialization when an unsafe collection class is used.

The issue described in the bug report relates to arbitrary remote code execution with `InvokerTransformer` used to build malicious serialized collections. This indicates the core problem is unsafe deserialization of arbitrary class types, especially when reflection-based instantiation is involved.

There is no evidence from the provided code snippets that the MultiValueMap or ReflectionFactory performs any security checks to whitelist or prevent certain class types from being instantiated via reflection. Thus, deserializing an instance created with a potentially unsafe class type like `String.class` does not throw the expected exception, causing the test to fail.

Summary:
- The test expects deserialization of a MultiValueMap that uses an unsafe class type (String.class) for its collection to throw `UnsupportedOperationException`.
- The MultiValueMap uses a ReflectionFactory that blindly instantiates classes via `clazz.newInstance()`.
- No validation or protective logic is visible to block or fail deserialization for unsafe collection class types.
- This causes the test to fail as unsafe classes are accepted during deserialization, posing security risks of code execution on deserialization.

Hence the bug happens because the deserialization process does not enforce any safety checks on the collection class used in the ReflectionFactory within MultiValueMap, leading to acceptance of unsafe types and enabling security exploits like arbitrary remote code execution during deserialization.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
